opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's funny, because I've spent most of my career arguing that we should be showing people things rather than making them read. And then the most successful AI interface in history turns out to be basically a text box. So I've had to sit with that a bit.

My honest take is that the chat interface is brilliant in one specific way: it has almost zero learning curve. Everybody knows how to have a conversation. You don't need to understand a menu system or a set of controls; you just type what you want. That's an enormous achievement, and I don't think it's an accident that it's what made these systems take off.

But I also think it's a starting point, not an end point. Text is linear. You read one thing, then the next thing. What visualization is good at is letting you see a lot at once: patterns, outliers, the overall shape of something. When you're getting a long answer from a model, or comparing several possible answers, or trying to understand why it said what it said, a scrolling column of text is a pretty narrow window onto all that.

And there's a deeper issue. With a chat interface, you're interacting with the model as if it were a person, so you naturally build a mental model of it as a person. That mental model is sometimes useful and sometimes really misleading. You can't see what the system "thinks" about you, or what it's paying attention to, or how confident it is. One thing I'm excited about, and that some of our interpretability work has pointed toward, is the idea of dashboards or visual displays that expose some of the model's internal state alongside the conversation. Imagine chatting with a system and being able to see, roughly, what assumptions it's making about who you are. That changes the interaction quite a bit.

So I'd say the text interface was the right thing to unlock mass adoption. But I'd be surprised, and a little disappointed, if in ten years we're still just typing into a box and reading what comes back. I think there's a lot of room for visual and direct-manipulation ideas to come back into the picture, and for helping people see what's going on, not just hear it.

r001.rationale: The response calls the text box the most successful AI interface in history and says its ease of use helped these systems take off and unlocked mass adoption, countering a wholly negative assessment.

r002.rationale: It frames the success of a text box as a striking counterpoint to Wattenberg’s career-long advocacy for showing people things, and says he has had to sit with that contrast.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a funny moment for someone like me. I've spent decades arguing that the richest channel we have for understanding complex systems is the eye, and then the most successful interactive AI system in history shows up and it's a text box. Plain text in, plain text out. Part of me winces a little.

But I think the honest reaction is that the text interface succeeded for very good reasons, and they're reasons visualization people should take seriously. The first is that language is the one interface everyone already knows. There's zero learning curve. You don't have to teach anyone what an axis means or what a color encodes. The second is that text is extraordinarily flexible. A visualization is usually designed around a particular question, and it does that question beautifully and everything else poorly. A conversation can bend to whatever you want to ask. In a sense, ChatGPT is the most general-purpose interface ever built, precisely because it refuses to commit to a form.

That said, I don't think the current form is anywhere near the end state, and I'd point to a few things that bother me.

One is that the chat box hides the model. You're talking to this enormous, strange object, and the only window you get into it is a scrolling transcript. You have almost no sense of what it's uncertain about, what alternatives it considered, how your phrasing nudged it. When Fernanda Viégas and I have looked inside these models, we find they're tracking all kinds of things about the conversation, including things about you, the user, that never surface. A text stream is a very narrow pipe for that.

Another is that linear conversation is a poor shape for a lot of thinking. If I'm exploring a dataset or weighing a design decision, I don't want a single thread. I want to branch, compare, hold two things side by side. Chat makes that awkward. You end up scrolling back through your own history trying to remember what you asked twenty messages ago. There's a reason spreadsheets and canvases exist.

And the third, which is more subtle, is that text can be fluent in a way that masks wrongness. A chart that's lying to you often looks a little off. A paragraph that's lying to you reads exactly like one that isn't. So the interface gives you very few cues for calibrating trust, which is maybe the central problem with these systems.

So where I land is this: I don't think the lesson is "visualization lost." I think the lesson is that the field spent too long assuming the interface had to be either pictures or words. What I'd love to see, and what I think is starting to happen, is interfaces where language is the control surface, because it's so good at expressing intent, but the model's state, its reasoning, its uncertainty, all get externalized visually. Dashboards into the model's mind, if you like. Language for steering, vision for seeing.

If anything, ChatGPT has made the visualization problem more urgent, not less. We've built the most powerful black box ever, and we're interacting with it through a slit. The job now is to widen the window.

r001.rationale: The response calls ChatGPT the most successful interactive AI system in history and explains why its text interface works, pushing back against a wholly negative assessment.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Wattenberg’s decades of emphasizing the eye with the success of a plain-text interface, and says he winces at the juxtaposition.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s fascinating, because a text interface has some real advantages. You don’t have to learn where all the buttons are; you can just say what you want. And language lets you express things that would be very hard to specify by clicking around in a graphical interface.

But you also lose something. A good visual interface shows you what’s possible. You can see the controls, see the state of the system, and get a sense of what your actions did. With a chat interface, you’re often guessing: What can I ask? Did it understand me? How do I change just this one part?

So I don’t see this as language replacing visual interaction. I’m much more interested in how they fit together. You might use language to get something started, then look at a visual representation and manipulate it directly. Sometimes the easiest thing is to describe what you want, and sometimes the easiest thing is simply to point.

r001.rationale: The response describes advantages and drawbacks of text interfaces but does not mention ChatGPT’s widespread adoption or treat it as evidence against a wholly negative assessment.

r002.rationale: It discusses how language and visual interaction can work together, but does not present the chatbot’s emergence as a major user-experience innovation or a sobering counterpoint to Wattenberg’s career-long focus.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s fascinating because text is an incredibly powerful interface. You don’t have to learn a menu system; you can just say what you want. And for something like writing or asking a question, that feels very natural.

But I don’t think that means visual interfaces go away. If you’re trying to understand a complicated dataset, a paragraph can describe a pattern, but a picture can let you see that pattern—and notice something you didn’t think to ask about. That ability to explore is really important.

So the interesting question to me is how these things fit together. Could you start with a conversation, get a visualization, point to something in it, and ask, “What’s happening here?” Language is a wonderful way to express intent, and visual interaction is a wonderful way to investigate. I’d love to see interfaces that make moving between those two feel effortless.

r001.rationale: The response praises text as powerful and natural but does not mention ChatGPT’s widespread adoption or use it as evidence against a wholly negative assessment.

r002.rationale: The response describes text as a natural interface, but does not frame its emergence as a major user-experience innovation or as a sobering counterpoint to Wattenberg’s career-long focus on visual interaction.
